passage: Tarun's mother was arriving on the 7:40 train, and at six the pressure cooker's whistle gave out. Neelam, who cooked faster, took over the dal on the small burner while her husband Tarun, who had the car and a free evening, drove to the station. The notebook on their fridge still showed what they had agreed last Sunday: she handled the rent transfer, he handled groceries and his mother's clinic visits, and they would look at it again next week. At dinner his mother watched Tarun clear the plates. "In our house, the boys never touched the kitchen." Neelam felt her jaw tighten. Tarun only smiled. "Amma, Neelam cooks better. I wash better." Later, holding a wet steel tumbler, his mother quietly asked him where the dish soap was kept.

qa.q: What time was Tarun's mother's train arriving?
qa.a: Her train was arriving at 7:40.

qa.q: What was Neelam feeling when her mother-in-law said the boys never touched the kitchen?
qa.a: Neelam felt irritated and a little defensive; her jaw tightened, though she let Tarun answer.

qa.q: What small habit helps this couple keep their split fair?
qa.a: Writing the agreement in a notebook and looking at it again each week keeps the split open to talk, so skill and time decide rather than old habits.

qa.q: How might Tarun's mother be seeing this way of running a home?
qa.a: It is unfamiliar to her and she voices the old rule, but asking where the dish soap is kept suggests she is slowly starting to adjust.

grounding: It illustrates a young couple sharing cooking, errands and money by skill and time, reviewing it regularly, and giving an elder room to adjust.

passage: Last winter a man on a grey scooter began slowing beside me on the lane from the metro to my hostel. Three evenings in a row. The third time he followed me past the tea stall, and I walked faster, pretending to talk on my phone. Chinmay, who runs the stationery shop there, stepped out and called loudly, "Didi, come inside, your order is ready." There was no order. The scooter left. I shook for a while among the notebooks. Next morning I told my warden and filed a complaint at the women's help desk; the officer noted the scooter's colour and the times without once asking what I had been wearing. I take the main road now, the one with lights. My name is Neelam, and I have stopped believing that route was my mistake.

qa.q: Where did Neelam report the man?
qa.a: She told her warden and filed a complaint at the women's help desk.

qa.q: What was Neelam feeling after the scooter left, and what shows it?
qa.a: She was frightened and shaken; she says she shook for a while among the notebooks even after the man had gone.

qa.q: Which responses in the passage helped, and why?
qa.a: Chinmay's quick made-up excuse got Neelam off the street without a fight, and reporting the scooter's colour and times gave the help desk facts to act on without any blame on her.

qa.q: How might Chinmay have seen the scene from the shop?
qa.a: Chinmay probably noticed the scooter trailing her and chose a calm, clever way to step in, offering a safe place instead of a confrontation.

grounding: It illustrates a young woman followed on her way home who is helped by a bystander, reports it without being blamed and now plans a safer route while knowing the fault is not hers.

passage:

Divyansh: saw a lady take 5 mins to park outside the mall 😅 this is why women shouldn't get licences
Rohit: haha
Divyansh: Akash where's your laugh
Akash: Nah. My sister drives me to work every day and hasn't scraped once. I've scraped twice.
Divyansh: bro it's a joke
Akash: I know. Just not a funny one to me. The lady was probably just parking carefully.
(Three minutes of nothing.)
Sameer: honestly my mum is the best driver in our house
Rohit: ok fair, my brother failed his test twice
Divyansh: fine fine. Akash, you're driving to the match tomorrow then 🙂
Akash: Deal. Pick you up at 4.

qa.q: Who drives Akash to work every day?
qa.a: His sister drives him to work every day.

qa.q: Why did Akash refuse to laugh, and what might he have felt typing his reply?
qa.a: He was uncomfortable with a joke that mocked women and probably a little nervous about spoiling the mood, yet sure enough to say so calmly.

qa.q: What made Akash's reply work in the group?
qa.a: He stayed calm, used a real example and did not insult Divyansh, so Sameer and Rohit felt free to agree instead of taking sides.

qa.q: How might Divyansh have felt when nobody replied for three minutes?
qa.a: Divyansh likely felt awkward and a bit exposed, then eased the tension by joking that Akash should drive, a sign he had taken the point.

grounding: It illustrates a young man who hears a joke about women drivers in a group chat and calmly objects, shifting what the group will laugh at.

subtopic: Caste and class awareness, discrimination recognition and fair conduct
passage: I'm Aparna, and I sit near the window in Class 4. I notice things. Francis always eats his lunch on the steps, not at our table. His mother cooks at our house in the mornings, and at school some boys call him "Francis-cook". He never answers. He just eats faster. One evening I asked Papa why Francis's mother makes our rotis but never sits on our sofa. Papa put his newspaper down. "She can sit wherever she likes. Aunty works for us; she is not less than us." The next morning he asked her to sit and have tea with him. I don't know what Francis feels about any of it. Today I carried my tiffin to the steps and sat down beside him.

qa.q: Where does Francis eat his lunch?
qa.a: Francis eats his lunch on the steps, not at the table.

qa.q: What might Aparna be feeling when asking Papa about the sofa?
qa.a: Aparna seems curious and a little uneasy, noticing something that feels unfair and wanting it explained.

qa.q: What did Papa's reply and action teach that a lecture could not?
qa.a: By saying she is not less and then inviting her to sit for tea, Papa showed fairness in action, and Aparna copied it the next day at school.

qa.q: What might it be like for Francis when some boys call him "Francis-cook"?
qa.a: It likely hurts and embarrasses him; he stays silent and eats faster, as if trying to get away from the teasing.

grounding: It illustrates a child noticing who sits apart, whose parent works in the house and whose name is teased, and how a parent's fair explanation shapes the child's own conduct.

subtopic: Caste and class awareness, discrimination recognition and fair conduct
passage: In a school yard in Porto, Noa pointed at Beatriz's worn trainers. "My uncle says people from the housing blocks are rubbish people." Noa said it the way you might say it could rain. Beatriz's face went stiff, and she walked off to the fence. Their teacher, Senhora Costa, had heard. She did not shout. She crouched beside Noa. "Look at Beatriz by the fence. How do you think those words landed?" Noa looked. "Sad?" "Yes. Where someone lives, or how much money a family has, does not make anyone worth less. Beatriz matters exactly as much as you." Noa scuffed a shoe on the ground. "My uncle says it all the time." "Grown-ups get things wrong too." After the break, Noa offered Beatriz half a custard tart.

qa.q: Who did Noa say uses those words all the time?
qa.a: Noa said the uncle says it all the time.

qa.q: What does Noa's casual tone suggest about how Noa felt saying it?
qa.a: Noa said it casually, like a remark about rain, and only guessed Beatriz felt sad when asked to look; the scuffed shoe suggests Noa then felt embarrassed.

qa.q: Why did Senhora Costa's approach work better than shouting?
qa.a: She stayed calm, got Noa to notice Beatriz's hurt and plainly explained that people are equal, so Noa could learn instead of just feeling scolded.

qa.q: What was it like for Beatriz to hear those words?
qa.a: It stung; her face went stiff and she walked off to the fence, hurt at being called rubbish because of where her family lives.

grounding: It illustrates a child repeating a class insult picked up from an uncle and a teacher's calm correction that names the hurt and explains that people are equal.

subtopic: Caste and class awareness, discrimination recognition and fair conduct
passage:
Thursday night.
Today in the lab Kunal put his bag on the empty stool and said, loud enough, "Not for you, Saurabh. Your lot clean drains, go stand over there." Two others laughed. I stood by the sink for the whole practical. My face was burning and my hands were cold. Dad has fixed the school's pipes for years. I am proud of him, and I still wanted to disappear.
Jeevan saw everything. After the bell, Jeevan walked with me straight to Mrs. Pillai's desk and said, "Ma'am, something happened in the lab that you need to hear." She listened to all of it, wrote it down and said, "I believe you. This is about what they said, not about you." She phoned Kunal's parents before the last period and is changing the seating plan from tomorrow.
Still feels heavy. But I was believed.

qa.q: Where did Saurabh stand for the whole practical?
qa.a: Saurabh stood by the sink for the whole practical.

qa.q: What was Saurabh feeling in the lab, and what shows it?
qa.a: Saurabh felt humiliated and hurt, with a burning face and cold hands, wanting to disappear while still proud of Dad.

qa.q: What did Jeevan do that a good friend could copy?
qa.a: Jeevan did not just sympathise later but went with Saurabh to the teacher straight after the bell, so the report was made the same day with a witness.

qa.q: How does Mrs. Pillai see what happened?
qa.a: She treats it as serious wrongdoing by the others, not Saurabh's fault: she believes the account, writes it down, phones Kunal's parents and changes the seating.

grounding: It illustrates a teenager mocked and refused a seat over family work, and how a peer and a teacher who believe and act support them.

subtopic: Caste and class awareness, discrimination recognition and fair conduct
passage: My name is Arohi. In the canteen on Tuesday the quota argument started again, and I was halfway to joining it. Hemant stood on a bench with his fist up, repeating a line from some video: "Merit is dead!" A few people cheered. I felt the heat of it in my own chest; it is easy to want a side. Then Pallavi, usually quiet, said her mother was the first in their village to finish school, and a reserved seat had made the difference. Nobody cheered for that. Someone else opened the government's own admission figures on a phone, and the numbers were messier than either slogan. Hemant climbed down. I can't say what he was thinking; his jaw was tight. I bought two teas and asked Pallavi to tell me more.

qa.q: What line was Hemant repeating on the bench?
qa.a: He was repeating "Merit is dead!"

qa.q: What was Arohi feeling as the canteen cheered, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Arohi felt a hot pull of excitement and anger, the heat in the chest that makes picking a side tempting.

qa.q: What did Arohi do that was wiser than joining a side?
qa.a: Arohi listened to Pallavi's lived story, noticed the real figures were messier than the slogans, and chose to keep asking questions over tea.

qa.q: How might Pallavi have experienced the canteen argument?
qa.a: Pallavi might have felt her family's real life was being turned into a slogan, and speaking quietly about her mother took some courage.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult drawn toward angry slogans in a quota debate who instead listens to lived experience and to data while staying respectful.

subtype: Hidden discrimination in work and housing [Receiver]
passage: Mehak, you asked why I keep every paper in that tin box. Let your Jagdish Chacha tell you. I was twenty, new in Pune, with a job letter in my pocket. The landlord was polite on the phone. At the door he asked my full surname, then whether we ate meat, then which district my people came from. That evening the room was "already given". Next day my friend Suresh phoned the same man and was offered it at once. I was angry enough to shout. Instead I wrote down every question with the date and time, and I asked Suresh to write down what he heard. A lawyer at the workers' union read my notes and sent a letter. I never lived there, beta. But the next tenant was asked no such questions.

qa.q: What three things did the landlord ask Jagdish at the door?
qa.a: He asked Jagdish's full surname, whether they ate meat, and which district his people came from.

qa.q: What was young Jagdish feeling when the room was suddenly "already given"?
qa.a: He was angry enough to shout, and probably hurt, sensing he had been judged by surname and food rather than by his job letter.

qa.q: At the turning point, why was writing things down wiser than shouting?
qa.a: Notes with dates, times and a second witness turned a suspicion into evidence that the union lawyer could act on.

qa.q: How might Suresh have felt when the landlord offered him the room at once?
qa.a: Suresh probably felt uncomfortable and indignant on Jagdish's behalf, and writing down what he heard made him a real ally.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult whose landlord asks about surname, food and region before refusing, and who documents it, finds an ally and seeks legal help.

subtopic: Caste and class awareness, discrimination recognition and fair conduct
passage: Ishita, sit, I'll tell you about Kamla-bai while the rice cooks. I was twenty-four and had just taken my first flat in Nagpur. In the house I grew up in, a separate steel cup for the helper hung on a nail by the back door. The first morning Kamla-bai came, I reached for that kind of cup out of habit, and then I stopped. I poured her tea into the same blue mugs I used. She held hers a long moment before drinking. I paid her on the first of every month, never the fifth, and I learnt her grandson's name. Small things. Eleven years she worked with me. When I moved away, she came to the station with laddoos. Remember that when you set up your own house, beta: your Vinita Maasi learnt it from a cup.

qa.q: On which day of the month did Vinita pay Kamla-bai?
qa.a: She paid her on the first of every month, never the fifth.

qa.q: Why did young Vinita stop reaching for the separate cup, and what does that suggest she felt?
qa.a: She seems to have felt uncomfortable, even a little ashamed, at copying an old habit that treated a person as lesser.

qa.q: Which small choice in the story mattered most, and why?
qa.a: Pouring tea into the same mugs mattered most because it showed daily respect, and paying on time and learning her grandson's name kept that respect going.

qa.q: How might Kamla-bai have felt holding the blue mug?
qa.a: She may have been surprised and quietly moved, as if being treated as an equal in a house was new to her.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult who uses the same cups, pays on time and treats the domestic helper as a person, showing daily conduct is where class prejudice ends.
